title: Design Playbook
scopeHtml: Scope: Latency budgets, reliability, fallbacks, scale and a framework for design questions.

notes.title: A framework for design questions
notes.html:
The seven-step structure (use it out loud in interviews).

  1. Clarify requirements.
    • Functional: users, tasks, inputs/outputs, languages, tools/actions, citations needed?
    • Non-functional: scale (users, requests/day, peak RPS), latency (TTFT, total), quality bar, availability, cost budget, security/privacy/compliance, residency.
    • Constraints: existing stack, team size, timeline.
  2. Define success metrics. Task success/resolution rate, accuracy/groundedness, latency, cost per task, safety rate, user satisfaction.
  3. Propose the simplest baseline. One prompt? Workflow? RAG? Agent? Justify the choice by predictability, data, risk.
  4. Draw the architecture and data flow. Ingestion, retrieval, generation, post-processing, storage, observability.
  5. Choose models and techniques. Model tiering and routing, API vs self-host, reasoning model or not, caching, structured outputs, fine-tuning only if justified.
  6. Quality, safety and evaluation. Eval set, guardrails, human fallback, red teaming, monitoring.
  7. Operations and trade-offs. Scaling, reliability, cost, rollout, risks, what you'd build later, what you'd measure.

Interview tips. Ask clarifying questions first; state assumptions with numbers; give a baseline then iterate; call out trade-offs explicitly ("I choose X over Y because…"); mention failure modes and mitigation; connect every component to a requirement.

Real life. An architect asks about the family and budget before drawing the house.

notes.title: Latency budgets
notes.html:
Method. Start from the user-facing target (e.g. first token < 1.5 s, total < 8 s for a streamed answer) and allocate a budget to each stage; measure p95, not averages.

Illustrative RAG chat breakdown (TTFT target 1.5 s).

Stage Budget
Network + auth + routing 100 ms
Input guardrails (parallel with next) 100 ms
Query rewrite (small model, optional) 250 ms
Embedding + hybrid search 150 ms
Rerank 150 ms
Prompt assembly 20 ms
LLM time to first token 600 ms
Slack / jitter 130 ms

Reduction techniques. Parallelize independent stages (BM25 + vector, guardrails + retrieval); skip rewriting when unnecessary; smaller models for auxiliary steps; prompt/prefix caching; shorter prompts; speculative decoding; streaming; regional deployment near users; warm instances; precomputation (summaries, embeddings); caching of frequent queries; avoid sequential tool calls where batch endpoints exist.

For agents. Latency = steps × (model + tool). Reduce steps via better tools/batching, parallel calls, plan-and-execute, smaller models for simple steps; show progress; allow async completion.

Real life. Planning a journey with time per leg and a buffer.

notes.title: Scaling
notes.html:
Capacity math. Required tokens/s = RPS × (avg input + avg output) per second. Compare against provider rate limits (RPM/TPM) or per-GPU throughput. Example: 100 RPS peak × 2,500 tokens = 250k tokens/s processed (mostly input); output 100 × 400 = 40k tokens/s — requires large capacity or negotiated limits and prompt caching to cut input cost.

Scaling levers.

  • Horizontal scaling of stateless services behind load balancers; autoscale on queue depth/latency.
  • Rate-limit aware clients: token-bucket per provider key, multiple accounts/regions, adaptive concurrency.
  • Queues and buffering to smooth bursts; priority classes (interactive vs batch).
  • Model tiering (small model handles the bulk).
  • Caching to cut calls.
  • Vector store scaling: sharding, replicas, partitioning by tenant, quantization.
  • Self-hosted inference: more replicas, continuous batching, tensor parallelism, autoscaling with warm pools.
  • Data pipeline scaling: parallel ingestion workers, batch embedding.

What breaks first at 10x. Provider rate limits → cost → vector store memory/latency → tail latency/queueing → observability volume → human review capacity. Plan each.

Real life. Sizing a motorway by rush-hour traffic, not the daily average.

notes.title: Reliability and fallbacks
notes.html:
Design for each failure.

Failure Mitigation
Primary provider outage / 5xx automatic failover to secondary provider/model (portable prompts, tested), or cached/simplified response
Rate limit 429 backoff + jitter, honor retry-after, queue, shift load to batch/secondary key, shed low-priority
Slow responses timeouts with deadline propagation, hedged requests for critical paths, smaller-model fallback
Malformed output validate, retry once with error, repair, fallback
Retrieval failure fall back to keyword search or no-RAG answer with disclaimer, or clarify
Tool failure retries, alternative tool, graceful message, partial results
Guardrail false positive safe refusal with appeal path, human review queue
Stream drop resume/retry, don't persist partial output

Principles. Define SLOs; one retry layer; circuit breakers; idempotency; graceful degradation to a non-AI path; regularly exercise failover; monitor error budgets.

Real life. A spare tyre you have actually checked.

notes.title: Cost trade-offs
notes.html:
Think in unit economics. Cost per request/resolution/user vs value created. Design levers in order of ease and safety: prompt/output trimming → prompt caching → retrieval instead of stuffing → model routing/cascades → batch APIs → distilled/fine-tuned small models → self-hosting at steady volume → hardware optimizations.

Trade-off examples.

  • Reranker adds 150 ms and a little cost but lets you pass 5 chunks instead of 20 (saves prompt tokens): often net positive.
  • Reasoning model improves hard-question accuracy but costs 5 to 20x per query: route only complex queries.
  • Semantic cache saves money but risks wrong answers: restrict to FAQs with strict thresholds.
  • Fine-tuning has upfront cost but removes 3k tokens of few-shot per call: pays back at volume.

Guardrails. Quotas, budgets, anomaly alerts, kill switches, forecasting; tie pricing to usage.

Real life. A shop watching margin per item, not just total sales.

notes.title: Worked example: customer-support assistant
notes.html:
Requirements. 50k conversations/day (peak 40 RPS), answers from the help centre and account data, EU residency, first token < 2 s, escalate to humans, audit trail.

Design.

  1. API layer: authenticated streaming chat endpoint, per-user rate limits, session store.
  2. Intent router (small model): FAQ vs account action vs complaint/escalation vs out-of-scope.
  3. Knowledge path (RAG): hybrid search (BM25 + vectors) over EU-region store, metadata filters (product, locale), cross-encoder rerank, top 5 chunks, "answer only from sources" prompt with citations, mid-size model; prompt caching for the static policy prefix.
  4. Action path: narrow tools (get_order_status, create_return_label) with per-user credentials; confirmation before state-changing actions; idempotency keys.
  5. Guardrails: PII redaction before logs, moderation, injection checks on retrieved/ticket text, output validation; low-confidence → human handoff with transcript summary.
  6. Reliability: provider failover to secondary EU model, timeouts, circuit breakers, degrade to FAQ search if LLM down.
  7. Observability: traces with versions, cost per conversation, groundedness sampling, escalation and CSAT dashboards.
  8. Evaluation: 500-case eval from historical tickets (including unanswerable, adversarial), CI gates, nightly runs, canary releases.
  9. Cost: routing keeps ~70% of traffic on a small model; estimate $0.01 to 0.03 per conversation; budgets per tenant.

Trade-offs discussed. RAG vs fine-tune (RAG for facts), long context vs retrieval (retrieval for scale/permissions), agent vs workflow (workflow with a router; agentic only for complex multi-step cases), build vs buy (managed vector DB initially).

Metrics. Resolution rate, containment, escalation precision, hallucination rate, p95 TTFT, cost per resolution, CSAT.

Real life. A well-run help desk with scripts, specialists and a supervisor for hard cases.

notes.title: Common mistakes
notes.html:
1. Jumping to agents (or multi-agent) when a workflow or single call suffices.
  2. No eval or tiny demo-driven validation.
  3. Ignoring cost until the bill arrives; no per-feature attribution.
  4. Trusting model output without validation; executing output unsafely.
  5. No fallbacks or untested failover.
  6. Unpinned model versions; no prompt versioning.
  7. Weak tenant isolation or permission checks in the prompt instead of retrieval.
  8. Stuffing context instead of retrieving; ignoring lost-in-the-middle.
  9. Skipping guardrails and red teaming.
  10. Treating prompts as static; no feedback loop.
  11. Over-engineering (complex frameworks, too many tools) before proving value.
  12. Ignoring latency tails and rate limits at scale.

Real life. Building a house without checking the foundations.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
Framework. Clarify requirements and constraints → success metrics → simplest baseline → architecture/data flow → models and techniques → quality/safety/eval → operations and trade-offs. Think aloud with numbers.

Latency. Budget per stage using p95; parallelize, cache, shrink prompts, tier models, stream; agents multiply steps, so cut steps and show progress.

Scaling. Convert RPS and token sizes into tokens/s, compare with provider limits or GPU throughput; queue and prioritize; rate-limit-aware clients; autoscale; plan what breaks first at 10x.

Reliability. Failover, backoff with jitter and retry-after, circuit breakers, validation and repair, degraded modes, tested drills, SLOs.

Cost. Unit economics; trim, cache, retrieve, route, batch, distil, self-host at volume; evaluate every optimization for quality.

Worked example. Support assistant with router, hybrid RAG + rerank + citations, narrow action tools with confirmation, guardrails, human handoff, failover, observability, evals and canaries, EU residency.

Mistakes to avoid. Agents by default, no evals, unmanaged cost, unvalidated outputs, no fallbacks, unpinned versions, weak isolation, context stuffing, no guardrails/feedback loops, over-engineering.

Interview one-liners.

  • "Start with the simplest thing that could work, and say why."
  • "Budget latency per stage, and show where the big term is."
  • "Every optimization is gated by the eval."
  • "Name the failure modes before the interviewer does."

questions.promptHtml: You get an open-ended "design a GenAI feature" question. What structure do you follow, and why do you not start by drawing boxes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They are testing whether you can turn a vague problem into requirements and numbers before proposing technology. Candidates who jump to "vector DB plus agent" fail here.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I follow seven steps: clarify requirements, define success metrics, propose the simplest baseline, draw the architecture and data flow, choose models and techniques, plan quality, safety and evaluation, then cover operations and trade-offs. An LLM (large language model) is a text-predicting model you call over an API, and every design choice depends on facts like traffic, latency target, risk and budget. So I ask about those first, like an architect asking about family and budget before drawing the house.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Step 1, clarify. Functional: who are the users, what inputs and outputs, which languages, does it need to take actions through tools, are citations required. Non-functional: scale (requests per day, peak RPS, meaning requests per second), latency (TTFT, time to first token, and total time), quality bar, availability, cost per task, privacy and data residency. Constraints: existing stack, team size, deadline.

Step 2, metrics: task success rate, groundedness (answer supported by sources), p95 latency (the value 95% of requests beat), cost per resolved task, safety rate, satisfaction. Without metrics you cannot say a design is good.

Step 3, simplest baseline: a single prompt, then a fixed workflow (a coded sequence of LLM calls), then RAG (retrieval-augmented generation: look up documents and put them in the prompt), and only then an agent (an LLM that decides its own next steps in a loop). Justify the choice by predictability, data availability and risk.

Steps 4 to 7 add the diagram (ingestion, retrieval, generation, post-processing, storage, observability), model tiering and caching, eval set and guardrails, and the operating story: scaling, reliability, rollout, risks and what you will measure.

requirements -> metrics -> baseline -> architecture -> models -> eval/safety -> ops/trade-offs
      ^                                                                              |
      +------------------ numbers and assumptions stated at every step --------------+

Say assumptions with numbers: "I assume 50k conversations a day, 40 RPS at peak, first token under 2 s." The interviewer can correct a number; they cannot correct a vague adjective.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Naming tools (Pinecone, LangChain) in the first minute.
  • Asking clarifying questions that do not change the design (ask only what would move a decision).
  • Presenting one architecture with no alternatives or "I choose X over Y because".
  • Forgetting failure modes and evaluation until the interviewer asks.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the interviewer refuses to give numbers? → State your own assumptions explicitly and say which would change the design.
  2. How do you decide between workflow and agent? → If the steps are known in advance, use a workflow; use an agent only when the path depends on intermediate results.
  3. Where do you spend the last five minutes? → Failure modes, rollout plan and what I would measure in week one.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: draws a RAG diagram with a vector database. Senior: spends the first third on requirements and metrics, starts with the simplest baseline, ties each component to a requirement and names trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team built a multi-agent assistant for an FAQ-sized problem; a router plus one RAG call would have met the same quality at a tenth of the latency and cost.

questions.promptHtml: What is TTFT, why do we design against p95 instead of average latency, and how do you set a latency budget?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Latency language (TTFT, percentiles, budgets) is basic vocabulary for GenAI products. Misusing averages is a common junior tell.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TTFT is time to first token: how long until the user sees the first word of a streamed answer. p95 means 95% of requests are faster than that number, so it shows what the slow tail feels like; averages hide it. I start from the user-facing target, say first token under 1.5 s, and split it into a budget per stage such as retrieval, rerank and model, with some slack, then measure each stage at p95.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
An LLM generates tokens (small chunks of text, roughly three-quarters of a word) one after another. With streaming the user sees tokens as they arrive, so two numbers matter: TTFT, which depends on everything before generation plus the model's prompt processing, and total time, which adds output length times per-token speed.

Why not the average: if 94 requests take 1 s and 6 take 12 s, the mean is 1.7 s, which looks fine, but 6% of users wait 12 s. Latencies are skewed with long tails, so use p95 or p99.

Budget method: start from the target and allocate. Illustrative RAG chat with a 1.5 s TTFT target: network and auth 100 ms, input guardrails 100 ms (in parallel), query rewrite 250 ms, embedding plus hybrid search 150 ms, rerank 150 ms, prompt assembly 20 ms, model TTFT 600 ms, slack 130 ms. Sequential stages add up; parallel stages cost the maximum, not the sum. The biggest term is where to optimize first.

|net|guard||rewrite|search|rerank|asm|--- LLM TTFT ---|slack|
 100  (par)   250     150    150   20       600          130   = 1.5 s

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reporting average latency to stakeholders.
  • Budgeting totals but not TTFT for streamed UIs.
  • Adding stage budgets that sum above the target.
  • Measuring only on a warm, idle system.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why p99 sometimes? → For fan-out systems and strict SLAs the tail dominates; each user request may hit many components.
  2. What shrinks TTFT most cheaply? → Streaming, shorter prompts, prompt caching, parallelizing independent stages.
  3. How do you measure per stage? → Tracing with spans per stage and p95 per span on a dashboard.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "we stream and use a fast model." Senior: allocates a per-stage budget, identifies the dominant term, reasons about parallel versus sequential stages and tracks tails per stage.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat feature showed a 1.8 s average but support tickets said it was "hanging"; p95 was 9 s because a reranker call occasionally queued behind batch jobs.

questions.promptHtml: An LLM API call returns 429 or a 5xx error. How should the client retry, and why add jitter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every GenAI app calls a rate-limited remote API. Naive retry loops turn small hiccups into outages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A 429 means "too many requests" (you hit a rate limit) and 5xx means the server failed. I retry only retryable errors, wait exponentially longer each time (exponential backoff), add random jitter so clients do not retry in sync, honor the retry-after header if present, cap attempts and total time, and do it in exactly one layer of the stack. Non-retryable errors like 400 or 401 fail immediately.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
If 1,000 clients all fail at the same instant and retry after exactly 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, they hit the server together each time, a thundering herd. Jitter randomizes the wait (for example a random value between 0 and the backoff ceiling, called full jitter) which spreads retries out.

Rules: respect retry-after (the server tells you when capacity returns); set a max attempts (3 to 5) and an overall deadline tied to the user's patience; retry only idempotent operations or use idempotency keys (a unique token so a repeated request is applied once), since a retried "send email" tool call must not send two emails. Official SDKs often retry by default; check so you do not stack retries (see the retry storm scenario).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import random, time

def call_with_retry(fn, max_attempts=4, base=0.5, cap=8.0):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        try:
            return fn()
        except RetryableError as e:           # your wrapper for 429 / 5xx / timeout
            if attempt == max_attempts - 1:
                raise
            delay = e.retry_after or random.uniform(0, min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt))
            time.sleep(delay)
suspend fun <T> callWithRetry(maxAttempts: Int = 4, base: Double = 0.5, cap: Double = 8.0, fn: suspend () -> T): T {
    repeat(maxAttempts) { attempt ->
        try { return fn() } catch (e: RetryableException) {
            if (attempt == maxAttempts - 1) throw e
            val ceiling = minOf(cap, base * Math.pow(2.0, attempt.toDouble()))
            delay(((e.retryAfterSeconds ?: (Math.random() * ceiling)) * 1000).toLong())
        }
    }
    error("unreachable")
}
static <T> T callWithRetry(Callable<T> fn, int maxAttempts, double base, double cap) throws Exception {
    for (int attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
        try { return fn.call(); }
        catch (RetryableException e) {
            if (attempt == maxAttempts - 1) throw e;
            double ceiling = Math.min(cap, base * Math.pow(2, attempt));
            double wait = e.retryAfterSeconds() != null ? e.retryAfterSeconds() : Math.random() * ceiling;
            Thread.sleep((long) (wait * 1000));
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Retrying 400 or 401 errors (they will never succeed).
  • Fixed-interval retries with no jitter.
  • Retrying at the SDK, the service, and the gateway at once.
  • Retrying non-idempotent tool actions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What do you do after max attempts? → Fall back (secondary provider, cached or simplified answer) or return a graceful error.
  2. Why a total deadline? → Five retries of 30 s each is a four-minute hang; the user left long ago.
  3. Is retry enough for sustained 429s? → No; you need queueing, rate-limit-aware clients and load shedding.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "retry three times with sleep." Senior: backoff plus jitter plus retry-after, one retry layer, deadlines, idempotency and a fallback after exhaustion.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A provider blip caused synchronized retries from 40 pods that kept the provider rate-limiting us for 20 minutes after the blip ended.

questions.promptHtml: How do you estimate whether your provider rate limits or your GPUs can handle a launch? Walk through the math.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Back-of-envelope capacity estimation separates people who have operated LLM systems from those who only prompted them.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I convert traffic into tokens per second: peak RPS times average input plus output tokens. A token is the unit LLMs read and write, about four characters of English. I compare that with the provider's limits, RPM (requests per minute) and TPM (tokens per minute), or with per-GPU throughput for self-hosting. I size for rush-hour peaks, not daily averages, and add headroom for retries and bursts.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example: peak 100 RPS, 2,500 input tokens and 400 output tokens per request. Input rate = 100 x 2,500 = 250,000 tokens/s, which is 15 million tokens per minute. Output rate = 100 x 400 = 40,000 tokens/s, 2.4 million per minute. Those are likely far above a default provider tier, so options are: negotiate limits or use multiple accounts and regions, cut input tokens (prompt caching of the static prefix, retrieval of fewer chunks), route easy traffic to a smaller model, or self-host.

Input and output are not equal: input is processed in parallel (prefill) and is cheaper per token; output is generated one token at a time (decode) and often dominates latency and per-GPU cost. Check which limit binds first, RPM, input TPM or output TPM.

Concurrency check by Little's law (in-flight requests = arrival rate x time in system): 100 RPS x 6 s per request = 600 concurrent requests. Your connection pools, worker threads and provider concurrency must allow that.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def required_capacity(rps, in_tok, out_tok, latency_s, headroom=1.3):
    return {
        "input_tps": rps * in_tok * headroom,
        "output_tps": rps * out_tok * headroom,
        "concurrency": rps * latency_s * headroom,
    }
print(required_capacity(100, 2500, 400, 6))
fun requiredCapacity(rps: Double, inTok: Int, outTok: Int, latencyS: Double, headroom: Double = 1.3) = mapOf(
    "input_tps" to rps * inTok * headroom,
    "output_tps" to rps * outTok * headroom,
    "concurrency" to rps * latencyS * headroom,
)
static Map<String, Double> requiredCapacity(double rps, int inTok, int outTok, double latencyS, double headroom) {
    return Map.of(
        "input_tps", rps * inTok * headroom,
        "output_tps", rps * outTok * headroom,
        "concurrency", rps * latencyS * headroom);
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Sizing from daily average traffic.
  • Ignoring that retries add load.
  • Treating input and output tokens as equal in cost and speed.
  • Forgetting concurrency limits (connections, threads).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you get peak from daily volume? → Measure the peak-to-average ratio from logs; a 3x to 10x factor is common for business-hour traffic.
  2. How does prompt caching change it? → Cached prefix tokens are cheaper and faster, but they usually still count toward some limits; check provider rules (verify).
  3. Self-host sizing? → Measure tokens/s per GPU under continuous batching with your real prompt shapes, then divide.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "we will scale up if needed." Senior: calculates tokens/s and concurrency, compares with the binding limit, lists levers and says what breaks first.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A launch passed load tests at 20 RPS but hit TPM limits at 70 RPS because the test used 600-token prompts while production prompts averaged 3,000.

questions.promptHtml: Your LLM bill is too high. In what order do you pull cost levers, and how do you decide each is safe?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior engineers own unit economics. They want an ordered, quality-aware plan, not "use a cheaper model".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: First measure cost per request and per resolution, attributed per feature. Then pull levers from easy and safe to hard: trim prompts and output, prompt caching, retrieval instead of stuffing context, model routing so a small model handles easy requests, batch APIs for offline work, distilled or fine-tuned small models, and only at steady high volume, self-hosting. Every change must pass the eval set so quality does not silently drop.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Unit economics means cost per unit of value: per conversation, per resolved ticket, per active user, compared with revenue or savings. Total spend alone hides whether the product is healthy.

Lever order and why:

  1. Trim prompts and cap output length: no quality risk when done carefully, immediate saving.
  2. Prompt caching: a long static prefix (policies, instructions, examples) is reused at a lower price and lower latency.
  3. Retrieve rather than stuff: send 5 relevant chunks, not a 50-page document.
  4. Route or cascade: a cheap model answers first; escalate to a strong model on low confidence or complex classes.
  5. Batch API: offline jobs (summaries, embeddings) at discounted price with delayed results.
  6. Distil or fine-tune a small model: upfront cost, pays back at volume (for example, removing 3k tokens of few-shot examples per call).
  7. Self-host at steady high utilization.

Trade-off examples: a reranker adds about 150 ms but lets you pass 5 chunks instead of 20, often a net saving; a reasoning model may cost 5 to 20x more per query, so route only hard queries; a semantic cache saves calls but risks wrong answers, so limit it to FAQs with strict similarity thresholds.

Guardrails: per-tenant budgets, quotas, anomaly alerts, a kill switch, spend forecasting.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Switching to a cheaper model without running the eval.
  • Optimizing the wrong feature because there is no per-feature cost attribution.
  • Caching personalized answers across users.
  • Self-hosting at low utilization where idle GPUs cost more than the API.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you attribute cost? → Tag every call with feature, tenant and prompt version; compute cost from token counts in traces.
  2. When does self-hosting win? → Predictable high volume, data control needs, and a team able to run inference infrastructure.
  3. How do you prove a cascade is safe? → Compare quality on a labelled set, per class, and monitor the escalation rate.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use a smaller model." Senior: measures first, orders levers by risk, gates each with the eval and puts budgets and kill switches in place.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team cut cost 35% by trimming a 4k-token system prompt and enabling prompt caching, with no model change and no quality drop on their eval.

questions.promptHtml: Explain timeouts with deadline propagation, circuit breakers and hedged requests. When do you use each for LLM calls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Slow responses are more common and more harmful than clean failures with LLM providers. They want proof you know the standard resilience toolkit.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A timeout limits how long you wait; deadline propagation passes the remaining time budget down through every call so no stage uses time the user no longer has. A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing, so you fail fast and fall back instead of piling up. A hedged request sends a second copy of a slow critical call after a short delay and takes whichever answers first. I use all three, but hedging only on critical, cheap-enough paths.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Timeout: an LLM call can hang for 60 s. Set the timeout from the user budget, for example 8 s total, and track the remaining deadline so the retry or fallback stage knows how much is left.

Circuit breaker: states closed (normal), open (calls blocked after error rate crosses a threshold, say 50% over 20 requests), half-open (after a cool-down, let a few probes through; success closes it). When open, route to the fallback immediately: secondary provider, smaller model, cached answer, or a non-AI path.

Hedging: if the p95 latency is 2 s, send a duplicate after 2 s to another replica or provider. This cuts the tail at the cost of extra load and tokens (around 5% more calls if you hedge only the slowest 5%). Do not hedge non-idempotent actions or expensive reasoning calls.

request -> [deadline 8s] -> primary --(slow >2s)--> hedge to secondary
                              |  error rate high
                           breaker OPEN -> fallback (small model / cache / FAQ search)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• One global timeout that ignores how much budget previous stages used.
  • A breaker with no fallback behind it (it just fails faster).
  • Hedging write actions.
  • Never testing the fallback until a real outage.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is hedging free? → No, it adds load and cost; limit to the tail and watch the hedge rate.
  2. How do you pick breaker thresholds? → From the SLO and observed baselines; tune with failure drills.
  3. How do you test failover? → Scheduled game days that block the primary in staging and a small share of production.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "add a timeout and a try/catch." Senior: propagates deadlines, pairs the breaker with a tested fallback, hedges selectively and drills regularly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: During a partial provider degradation (not an outage) requests stalled for 45 s; teams with 8 s deadlines and a breaker degraded gracefully, others saw thread pools exhaust.

questions.promptHtml: Why is "jumping straight to agents" listed as a classic design mistake, and how do you decide between a single call, a workflow and an agent?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Agents are fashionable. Interviewers want judgment about when added autonomy is worth its cost in latency, money and unpredictability.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A single call is one prompt; a workflow is a fixed coded sequence of calls, like route, retrieve, answer; an agent is an LLM looping and choosing its own tools and steps. Agents multiply latency, cost and failure modes because each step is another model call plus a tool call, and results become harder to test. I pick the simplest one that meets the quality bar: single call, then workflow, and an agent only when the path really depends on intermediate results.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Agent latency is steps x (model time + tool time). With 8 steps, 2 s model plus 1 s tool each, that is 24 s. Errors compound too: with 95% reliability per step, 8 steps give about 0.95^8 = 66% end-to-end success.

Decision guide:

  • Single call: classification, extraction, summarization, short Q&A. Cheapest, easiest to eval.
  • Workflow (router, prompt chain, parallel branches): known steps, such as support intent routing then RAG. Predictable, testable per step.
  • Agent: open-ended problems (debug a failing build, research task) where you cannot enumerate the steps. Add step limits, budgets, tool permissions and human approval for risky actions.

Hybrid is common: a workflow with an agentic branch only for the complex 10% of traffic.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Multi-agent frameworks for problems a router solves.
  • No step or cost cap on agent loops.
  • Skipping evals because "the agent figures it out".
  • Giving agents broad tools instead of narrow, permissioned ones.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you cut agent latency? → Fewer steps via better tools and batching, parallel tool calls, plan-and-execute, smaller models for simple steps, progress UI, async completion.
  2. How do you make an agent safe? → Narrow tools, per-user credentials, confirmations for state changes, step and budget caps.
  3. When is multi-agent justified? → Distinct contexts or skills that would overflow one prompt; prove it with an eval versus a single agent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "an agent can handle anything." Senior: computes compounded error and latency, defaults to a workflow, and constrains agents with limits and approvals.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 5-agent pipeline had a 22 s median and a 60% task success; replacing it with a router plus RAG workflow gave 3 s and 85% on the same eval.

questions.promptHtml: Compare model routing, cascades and semantic caching as cost levers. What are the failure modes of each and how do you guard them?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: These three are the most common "senior" cost answers, and each has a quality trap. They want to hear the traps.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Routing picks a model up front based on the request (a cheap classifier decides easy versus hard). A cascade tries a cheap model first and escalates if a confidence check fails. A semantic cache returns a stored answer when a new query's embedding (a numeric vector representing meaning) is very close to an old one. All three save money but can silently lower quality or return wrong answers, so each needs eval gating, thresholds and monitoring of misroutes and cache hits.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Routing: cost of the router (one small call, 100 to 200 ms) must be below the saving. Failure mode: misrouting hard queries to the weak model. Guard: evaluate per class, bias toward the strong model when uncertain, log router decisions and sample for review.

Cascade: cheap first, then verify. Failure mode: the cheap model is confidently wrong so the confidence check never triggers, and escalations add latency (two sequential calls). Guard: use a verifier or calibrated signals (not just self-reported confidence), track escalation rate; if it climbs to 60%, the cascade costs more than the strong model alone.

Semantic cache: embed the query, find a neighbour above a similarity threshold, and return its stored answer. Failure modes: near-duplicates with different meaning ("cancel my order" vs "do not cancel my order"), personalized or time-sensitive answers served to the wrong user, stale answers after a policy change. Guard: restrict to FAQ-like public content, strict thresholds validated on labelled pairs, tenant and locale in the cache key, TTL and invalidation on source updates.

Expected value check: saving = hit rate x cost per call; risk = hit rate x wrong-hit rate x cost of a wrong answer. Include the risk term.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Setting the cache threshold by intuition (0.85) without a labelled set.
  • Caching answers that depend on the user's account data.
  • Counting savings but not the extra latency of routing or escalation.
  • Not versioning cache entries by prompt and model version.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Exact-match cache versus semantic? → Exact-match is safe and cheap; add semantic only after measuring repeated paraphrases.
  2. How do you measure router quality? → Confusion matrix against human-labelled difficulty, plus end-to-end task success per route.
  3. Can the cache leak data? → Yes, across tenants if the key omits tenant; always scope keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cache similar questions to save money." Senior: models the wrong-hit risk, scopes keys, validates thresholds on labelled data and monitors drift.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A semantic cache served a pricing answer from before a plan change for two weeks until invalidation hooks were tied to the content pipeline.

questions.contextHtml: A product manager says: "Build an AI assistant for HR so employees can ask questions. We want it live in six weeks." There is a 400-document policy library (PDFs and wiki pages), 8,000 employees in 3 countries, an existing SSO login, and a two-engineer team. No budget number, no quality bar and no list of what the assistant may do beyond "answer questions".
questions.promptHtml: How do you respond in the first meeting, and what do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts naming a vector database and an agent framework immediately, or asks 25 unfocused questions. It never defines what "good" means or whether the assistant should take actions like submitting leave requests.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Read-only answers or also actions (leave requests)? Actions change risk and tooling. (b) Which countries and languages, and do policies differ by country? That drives metadata filtering. (c) Expected volume and peak (8,000 employees might mean 500 questions a day)? Drives cost and scale. (d) What is the cost of a wrong answer (legal, payroll)? Drives refusal and human escalation. (e) Data residency and who may see which documents (managers versus staff)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident; I lock scope instead. I propose phase 1: read-only Q&A with citations over the policy library for one country.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the baseline that fits is RAG (retrieval over documents) with a mid-size model; an agent is unnecessary for read-only Q&A; fine-tuning is not needed for facts that change.
  4. How I'd verify each: Build a 100-question eval set with HR collecting real questions, including unanswerable and sensitive ones; measure groundedness and correct refusal rate.
  5. Root cause: The real risk is the ambiguity itself; the stated requirement has no metrics.
  6. Fix: Written success metrics: at least 85% correct-with-citation on the eval, p95 first token under 2 s, escalation to HR for low-confidence or sensitive topics, cost under an agreed amount per question.
  7. Prevention: A weekly review of sampled conversations, and a feedback button feeding the eval set.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not build actions (leave submission) in the first six weeks, nor use a custom model; those can follow once read-only quality is proven.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The PM insists on leave requests in phase 1. → Add one narrow tool with user-scoped credentials, confirmation before submit and idempotency keys, but keep it behind a flag until the eval passes.
  • HR says some documents are confidential to managers. → Enforce permissions in retrieval filters using the SSO identity, never in the prompt.
  • Quality is 70% at week 4. → Cut scope (fewer topics), improve chunking and retrieval, add a reranker, and widen the refusal.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team shipped an HR bot without a refusal path; it confidently answered a parental-leave question using an outdated country policy, and the retraction cost more than the missing eval would have.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: jumps to tools, never asks about risk, metrics or actions.
  • Hire: asks targeted questions, proposes read-only RAG with an eval set and citations.
  • Strong hire: also sets numeric success criteria, permission enforcement in retrieval, phased scope and a plan to change scope if quality misses.

questions.contextHtml: A RAG chat assistant has a target TTFT (time to first token) of 1.5 s at p95, but production p95 is 3.4 s (p50 is 1.4 s). Tracing shows p95 per stage: gateway and auth 120 ms, input moderation 450 ms, query rewrite with a mid-size model 900 ms, embedding plus vector search 180 ms, BM25 search 140 ms, rerank of 50 chunks 600 ms, prompt assembly 30 ms, LLM TTFT 800 ms. All stages run one after another. 30% of queries are follow-ups ("and what about Germany?").
questions.promptHtml: What do you change to hit 1.5 s, and in what order?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a faster model" or "add caching" without looking at the stage numbers; the LLM is only 800 ms of 3,220 ms.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is quality tied to rewrite and rerank (check the eval before removing)? Is the 1.5 s target at p95 for all users or a region? Can moderation run asynchronously with streaming held until it passes?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stream tokens, and cut the rerank candidates from 50 to 20 as a quick win if the eval allows.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the sum is 120+450+900+180+140+600+30+800 = 3,220 ms, so the culprits are rewrite (900), rerank (600) and moderation (450), and the sequential layout.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-run the 500-question eval with each change; compare recall at 5, groundedness and p95 per stage in traces.
  5. Root cause: Everything is sequential and auxiliary steps use heavy models.
  6. Fix: (a) Run moderation in parallel with retrieval: saves about 450 ms. (b) Run vector and BM25 in parallel: max(180,140) saves 140 ms. (c) Rewrite only for follow-ups (30% of traffic) and use a small model, about 250 ms. (d) Rerank 20 chunks with a faster reranker, about 150 ms. New p95 path: 120 + max(450 moderation, rewrite 250 + search 180 + rerank 150 = 580) + 30 + 800 = about 1,530 ms. Then trim prompt length and use prompt caching on the static prefix to bring the LLM TTFT down toward 600 ms.
  7. Prevention: A per-stage latency budget in CI performance tests and alerts on any stage exceeding 120% of budget.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not drop the reranker entirely without an eval, since it saved prompt tokens and improved precision; I would not hide latency only with a spinner.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Quality drops 3 points after rerank cut. → Try 30 candidates, or a distilled reranker; accept a budget slip only if the quality gain is worth it.
  • p50 is fine but p95 is bad. → Look for queueing and cold starts; warm instances, check retry paths.
  • Moderation must complete before any output. → Run it parallel to retrieval and hold the stream until it passes; the model still starts earlier.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent a month swapping LLMs for 100 ms gains; one trace showed a query-rewrite call burning 900 ms on queries that did not need it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes generic speedups without using the stage numbers.
  • Hire: parallelizes stages, conditionally rewrites, shrinks rerank, recomputes the total.
  • Strong hire: also verifies with an eval, adds budgets to CI and discusses tail causes.

questions.contextHtml: At 14:05 your single LLM provider starts returning 503 errors for 40% of requests, with the other 60% taking 25 to 40 s. Your app (30 RPS) has an 8 s timeout and three retries. Within 5 minutes, your worker pool is saturated, even the health-check endpoint is slow, and the support chat shows spinners. The status page says "investigating". There is no secondary provider configured.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do right now, and what should have existed?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wait for the provider" or "increase the retries". More retries raise load and make saturation worse.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which features depend on the LLM versus a non-AI path? Is a secondary model or region approved by security and legal? Which tenants are in contractual SLA?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Open the circuit breaker manually, lowering retries to 0, and shed load. Switch chat to a degraded mode: FAQ keyword search and a banner, with an option to create a human ticket. Free the worker pool by enforcing the 8 s deadline.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: provider partial outage (most likely given status page), our own retries amplifying (3 retries x 8 s x 30 RPS), a regional network issue.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check error rates by status code and region from our traces; call the provider from a separate host with a curl probe; compare retry counts per request.
  5. Root cause: A single point of failure plus unbounded waiting: slow responses (not errors) hold threads, and retries multiply requests by up to 4x.
  6. Fix: Short term: breaker plus fallback as above. Long term: a secondary provider or model behind a gateway with portable, tested prompts; separate thread pools or async IO so health checks never starve; per-request deadlines propagated everywhere.
  7. Prevention: SLOs and error budgets, quarterly failover drills, synthetic canary calls that measure provider health, and a runbook.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not blindly fail over to an unevaluated model for regulated answers; a degraded safe response beats a wrong one. I would not stack retries.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Secondary model gives 8-point lower quality. → Use it only during incidents with a disclaimer and restrict to low-risk intents.
  • Prompts use provider-specific features. → Keep a thin adapter and tested equivalents; accept some feature loss in fallback mode.
  • Data residency forbids the second provider. → Choose a secondary within the same region or degrade to non-AI paths.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: During one provider incident, the team with a practiced failover restored service in 6 minutes; the team that had "planned" it discovered their fallback prompts returned malformed JSON.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: waits or increases retries.
  • Hire: opens the breaker, degrades to a non-AI path, notes missing redundancy.
  • Strong hire: also analyses retry amplification and pool starvation, proposes drills, SLOs and a tested portable failover.

questions.contextHtml:
After a deploy, a provider hiccup (429s for 90 seconds) turns into a 15-minute outage of your own service. Three layers each retry: the provider SDK (default 2 retries), your service wrapper (3 retries, fixed 1 s sleep), and the API gateway in front of it (2 retries on any 5xx). Code of the wrapper:

def ask(prompt):
    for _ in range(3):
        try:
            return client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500,
                                          messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
        except Exception:
            time.sleep(1)
    raise RuntimeError("failed")
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, what is the worst-case amplification, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the sleep." That misses the stacked layers and the catch-all exception.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are the SDK retries configurable? Does the gateway retry POSTs? Are tool actions involved (non-idempotent)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set the SDK max_retries to 0, disable gateway retries for this route, and shed traffic.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: stacked retries (primary), fixed sleep without jitter (synchronized waves), catching Exception so 400 and 401 errors are retried as well.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count upstream provider requests per user request in traces; read SDK docs for default retry settings (verify); inspect the logs for repeated 400s.
  5. Root cause: Worst case per user request: gateway 3 attempts x wrapper 3 attempts x SDK 3 attempts = 27 provider calls. At 20 RPS that is up to 540 calls/s against a service already rate-limiting you.
  6. Fix: Exactly one retry layer. Retry only 429, 5xx and timeouts, with exponential backoff and jitter, honor retry-after, set an overall deadline, and stop on 4xx.
  7. Prevention: A design rule "one retry layer per hop", a load test that injects 429s, and a metric for upstream calls per request.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not retry at the gateway for POSTs that cause side effects, and I would not hide failures by retrying forever.
client = anthropic.Anthropic(max_retries=0)    # verify parameter name in the SDK docs

def ask(prompt, deadline=time.monotonic() + 8):
    for attempt in range(3):
        try:
            return client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500,
                                          messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
        except (anthropic.RateLimitError, anthropic.APIConnectionError, anthropic.InternalServerError) as e:
            wait = random.uniform(0, 0.5 * 2 ** attempt)
            if attempt == 2 or time.monotonic() + wait > deadline:
                raise
            time.sleep(wait)
// One retry layer: configure the client with 0 SDK retries (verify option in the Java SDK docs)
// and keep the loop below as the only retry.
suspend fun ask(prompt: String, deadlineMs: Long): Message {
    for (attempt in 0 until 3) {
        try { return client.messages().create(params(prompt)) }
        catch (e: RetryableException) {                    // your wrapper for 429/5xx/timeouts only
            val wait = (Math.random() * 500 * (1 shl attempt)).toLong()
            if (attempt == 2 || System.currentTimeMillis() + wait > deadlineMs) throw e
            delay(wait)
        }
    }
    error("unreachable")
}
// Same shape: SDK retries off (verify), single wrapper retry on 429/5xx/timeouts only.
Message ask(String prompt, long deadlineMs) throws Exception {
    for (int attempt = 0; ; attempt++) {
        try { return client.messages().create(params(prompt)); }
        catch (RetryableException e) {
            long wait = (long) (Math.random() * 500 * (1 << attempt));
            if (attempt == 2 || System.currentTimeMillis() + wait > deadlineMs) throw e;
            Thread.sleep(wait);
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Can the gateway keep its retry? → Only if the app layer has none; otherwise choose the layer that knows the deadline and idempotency.
  • Why jitter if there is a single client? → There are many pods; synchronized waves hit together.
  • How do you stop a storm while the provider recovers? → Circuit breaker plus load shedding.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "harmless" gateway retry setting multiplied by two other layers quietly produced a 27x traffic amplification that only showed during a provider incident.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweaks the sleep.
  • Hire: finds the stacked layers and the catch-all, proposes one layer with jitter.
  • Strong hire: computes the 27x amplification, adds deadlines, breaker and a test that injects failures.

questions.contextHtml: Monthly LLM spend jumps from $18k to $54k with traffic up only 10%. There is one shared API key across five features (chat, summaries, search rewrite, an internal agent, batch tagging). Logs only record total tokens per day. Average input tokens per call rose from 2,100 to 4,900. A recent change added a "company policy" block to every prompt, and an agent loop sometimes runs 20+ steps.
questions.promptHtml: How do you find the cause, stop the bleeding, and prevent a repeat?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to a cheaper model." Without attribution it may hit the wrong feature and degrade quality.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: When did the spike begin (a deploy or traffic)? Which features have their own spend? Are caching and batching currently enabled? Any customers with unusual usage?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set a hard budget cap and a per-feature rate limit, cap agent steps (for example 8), and split API keys per feature to get instant attribution.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The policy block added about 2,800 tokens to every prompt (matches the input increase, 4,900 minus 2,100). (b) Runaway agent loops. (c) A feature creating duplicate calls (retries). (d) Traffic mix shifting to heavier features. Red herring: the 10% traffic growth cannot explain 3x.
  4. How I'd verify each: Join traces by feature, prompt version and token counts; histogram agent steps per run; compare calls per user request before and after the deploy.
  5. Root cause (typical): A static 2.8k-token block sent uncached on every call, plus an unbounded agent loop. 2.33x input growth times 1.1 traffic times extra agent output approximates the 3x bill.
  6. Fix: Short term: enable prompt caching on the static prefix, trim the block, cap steps. Long term: per-feature tags and dashboards (cost per request, per resolution), model routing for simple calls, batch API for tagging.
  7. Prevention: Cost per request alerts by feature, prompt-size CI check (fail if over a token budget), spend anomaly alerts and a kill switch.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not remove the policy block blindly (it may be required); cache it. I would not lower max output tokens globally as it can truncate answers.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Caching cuts cost but latency rises. → Check cache misses due to prompt changes before the prefix; keep the static part first.
  • Finance wants a forecast. → Cost per task x projected tasks, with scenarios for the traffic mix.
  • One tenant caused 40% of cost. → Per-tenant quotas, pricing tied to usage.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A single sentence added to a shared system prompt multiplied cost for six weeks because nobody tracked tokens per request by prompt version.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: swaps models without data.
  • Hire: asks for attribution, finds the prompt growth and loops, adds caps.
  • Strong hire: also uses cost per request alerts, prompt budgets in CI, caching and routing, with eval gating.

questions.contextHtml: A support assistant runs 5 RPS average and 15 RPS peak (average 2,500 input and 400 output tokens, p95 TTFT 1.4 s, cost $0.02 per conversation). Marketing announces a launch that should bring 10x traffic in three weeks: 150 RPS peak. Today's provider tier allows 4 million input tokens/minute. The vector store has 3 million chunks on one node at 70% memory, and humans review 3% of conversations (6 reviewers).
questions.promptHtml: What will break first at 10x, and how do you prepare?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Autoscale the pods." Pods are stateless and are not the bottleneck.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 150 RPS a hard peak or a burst? Can the launch be staged by region? Is there budget for higher tiers? What must not degrade (latency, quality, escalation)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Request the limit increase from the provider now (lead time can be weeks); prepare a queue with priority classes.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (what breaks first): (1) Provider limits: 150 RPS x 2,500 = 375,000 tokens/s = 22.5M tokens/min versus the 4M limit, a 5.6x gap. (2) Cost: $0.02 x 10 = a 10x bill, unless reduced. (3) Vector store memory: 70% used with growth plus replicas. (4) Tail latency from queueing. (5) Observability volume. (6) Human review: 3% of 10x traffic is 10x the work.
  4. How I'd verify each: Load test with production-shaped prompts at 2x, 5x, 10x; run capacity math; measure vector search p95 under load; watch queue depth.
  5. Root cause: Capacity was designed for linear low traffic with every limit hand-tuned.
  6. Fix: Cut input tokens (prompt caching on the policy prefix, 5 chunks instead of 10 after rerank), route 70% of traffic to a small model, multi-key or multi-region provider accounts with a rate-limit-aware client (token bucket), shard or replicate the vector store and add quantization, sample human review (1% plus low-confidence triggers) and add autoscaling on queue depth.
  7. Prevention: Quarterly capacity reviews, load tests in CI before big launches, alerts at 70% of any limit.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not hit the limit and rely on 429 retries; I would not cut human review to zero; I would not launch globally on day one.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The limit increase is denied. → Stage the launch, use queued or batch paths for non-urgent traffic, self-host a smaller model for the bulk.
  • Peak is 3x higher than estimated. → Load shedding with priorities and a degraded FAQ mode.
  • Cost target stays at $0.02. → Routing and caching targets must be verified with the eval first.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team load-tested the web tier to 10x and celebrated; the provider limit was 5x lower than the launch traffic, found at 09:02 on launch day.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale pods.
  • Hire: does token math and finds the rate limit gap.
  • Strong hire: ranks the full chain (limits, cost, vector store, tail, observability, humans), with mitigation, staging and load tests.

questions.contextHtml: Design the AI layer for a customer-support assistant: 50k conversations a day (peak 40 RPS), answers from the help centre (12,000 articles) plus account data (orders, returns), EU data residency, first token under 2 s, human escalation, and a full audit trail. The CTO asks for "an autonomous agent that can do everything".
questions.promptHtml: Walk through your design and push back on the CTO's request where needed.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: One giant agent with every tool and the whole help centre pasted into the prompt, with no routing, evals or guardrails.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which actions (refund, return label) are allowed and who approves? What containment rate and CSAT are targeted? Which languages? Is a provider with an EU region approved?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Start with a read-only knowledge path in a pilot while the action tools get security review.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (design choices): Workflow with a router beats a single agent; RAG beats fine-tuning for facts; retrieval beats long context for scale and permissions.
  4. How I'd verify each: A 500-case eval from historical tickets (including unanswerable and adversarial), CI gates, nightly runs, canary releases.
  5. Root cause: n/a (design); the key insight is separating knowledge, actions and escalation paths.
  6. Fix (the design): (a) Streaming API with auth, per-user rate limits and a session store. (b) A small-model intent router: FAQ, account action, complaint or out-of-scope. (c) Knowledge path: hybrid search (BM25 plus vectors) in an EU-region store with product and locale filters, cross-encoder rerank, top 5 chunks, "answer only from sources" prompt with citations, prompt caching on the static prefix. (d) Action path: narrow tools such as get_order_status and create_return_label with per-user credentials, confirmation before state changes, idempotency keys. (e) Guardrails: PII redaction before logging, moderation, prompt-injection checks on retrieved text, output validation, low confidence goes to a human with a transcript summary. (f) Reliability: failover to a secondary EU model, timeouts, breakers, FAQ search as the degraded mode. (g) Observability: traces with versions, cost per conversation, groundedness sampling, CSAT.
  7. Prevention: Canary releases, pinned model and prompt versions, red-team suite.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not one autonomous agent; agentic behaviour only for complex multi-step cases after the workflow proves itself. Expected cost: routing keeps about 70% of traffic on a small model, around $0.01 to 0.03 per conversation (estimate; verify with real token counts).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Legal wants every answer reviewed. → Review a risk-based sample; hold only high-risk intents for human approval.
  • Help centre updates daily. → Incremental re-indexing with document versions and freshness metadata.
  • Providers lack EU region for the best model. → Use the best EU-resident option and measure the quality gap on the eval.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A support bot with permission checks written in the prompt leaked one customer's order to another; the fix moved authorization into the tool layer.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: single agent, no eval or guardrails.
  • Hire: router, hybrid RAG with citations, narrow tools, escalation.
  • Strong hire: also covers residency, cost math, failover, evals, canaries, and clear pushback on the autonomous-everything request.

questions.contextHtml: Every weekday 09:00 to 09:20 your service sees 429 rate-limit errors for 25% of requests. Daily average is only 8 RPS, but the 09:00 spike reaches 45 RPS. Three traffic types share one provider key: interactive chat (users waiting), a nightly-catch-up summarizer that someone scheduled at 09:00, and a bulk document tagger. TPM usage touches 100% of the limit for twenty minutes, then falls to 15%. Interactive p95 goes from 1.5 s to 11 s.
questions.promptHtml: How do you fix this without simply buying a bigger limit?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Request a higher limit" (maybe needed, but it ignores the bulk jobs competing with interactive traffic).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which jobs can be delayed? Can the summarizer run at night? Is the limit per key, per organization, per model? Any batch API discount available?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pause the summarizer and tagger during 09:00 to 09:30 and rate-limit them.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Batch jobs competing with interactive traffic (timing matches). (b) Retries inflating load during 429 bursts. (c) A prompt size regression. Red herring: average RPS at 8 looks harmless; the peak matters.
  4. How I'd verify each: Break down tokens per minute by traffic type from traces, count retries per request, compare prompt sizes before and after.
  5. Root cause: One shared budget with no priorities, so low-value bulk work starved interactive users.
  6. Fix: Priority queues: interactive gets reserved capacity (for example 60% of TPM); bulk jobs use a token bucket in the client and run off-peak or via a batch API (results within hours, lower price, verify); separate keys or projects per class; adaptive concurrency that backs off on 429; load shedding with a friendly message for the lowest-priority interactive requests only as a last resort.
  7. Prevention: Alerts at 70% of TPM, a scheduler review for any new job, per-class dashboards.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not unlimited retries; not buying capacity before fixing priorities, because the next bulk job will eat it.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interactive alone exceeds the limit at 09:00. → Then ask for more capacity, add a smaller-model route, reduce prompt tokens and queue with a visible wait.
  • The bulk job has a deadline of 10:00. → Batch API or run at 03:00.
  • Multiple keys? → Check terms of service; use proper tiers or multiple projects, not tricks.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An innocent cron job was added by another team at 09:00; the incident was a scheduling collision, not a capacity problem.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: asks for a bigger limit only.
  • Hire: separates traffic classes and moves bulk work off-peak.
  • Strong hire: priority queues with reserved capacity, token buckets, retry analysis and alerts.

questions.contextHtml: On a Tuesday, JSON parse failures in your extraction service jump from 0.4% to 9% and support-ticket routing accuracy drops from 94% to 81%. No code deploy happened. The code calls a model by a floating alias ("latest"), the prompt lives in a database edited through an admin page with no history, and the eval suite is run manually "when someone remembers". The provider released an update to the alias that morning. Rollback took 5 hours because nobody knew which prompt text was running last week.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review: causes, fixes and what you change in the process.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the provider. The provider behaved as documented; the team's lack of pinning, versioning and evals made them vulnerable.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did the prompt change that week? Which model version served the failing requests (logged)? What does the eval say on the new version? How was the alias documented?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Pin to the last known-good dated model version and restore the previous prompt text from backups or logs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Floating alias moved to a new model with different formatting behaviour. (b) An unrecorded prompt edit. (c) A schema or input data change. Red herring: traffic volume was normal.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check provider response metadata for the model id per request; diff prompts via audit logs; replay 200 saved requests on old versus new model.
  5. Root cause: Unpinned model, unversioned prompt and no automated eval gate; any one control would have caught or limited the failure.
  6. Fix: Pin dated model versions; store prompts in git or a versioned registry with the version tagged on every trace; add structured outputs or schema validation with one retry and a fallback; run the eval in CI and nightly against production configuration.
  7. Prevention: Canary releases for model upgrades with a quality gate, alerts on parse-failure rate, and an upgrade calendar to deliberately test new versions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "never upgrade"; pinned versions get deprecated, so plan migrations. Blameless tone: fix the system, not the person.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The pinned version is being deprecated in 60 days. → Run the eval on candidates, fix prompts, canary 5% then 50% then 100%.
  • Eval takes 40 minutes in CI. → Run a small smoke set per PR and the full set nightly.
  • Can validation fully prevent this? → It limits damage, but accuracy drops need an eval to detect.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A silent alias update changed a model's tendency to wrap JSON in markdown fences; the parser broke for five hours because nobody could tell what had changed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the vendor, asks for a rollback only.
  • Hire: pins versions, versions prompts, adds validation and evals.
  • Strong hire: includes canary upgrade process, version tagging in traces, blameless review and a deprecation plan.

questions.contextHtml: Your analyst-assistant answers 200k queries a month. A mid-size model costs about $0.012 per query and gets 78% on your eval. A reasoning model (spends extra "thinking" tokens before answering) gets 91% but costs about $0.14 per query (illustrative numbers; verify current prices) and adds 8 s of latency. Product wants the best accuracy. Finance wants the bill under $8k a month. Your query log shows 25% of queries are hard multi-step questions, the rest lookups and simple summaries.
questions.promptHtml: What architecture do you propose, and how do you justify it with numbers?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Pick one model for everything, either too costly ($28k per month for all-reasoning) or too inaccurate.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How is "hard" defined and can it be labelled? What is the cost of a wrong answer on hard queries? Can hard queries tolerate 8+ s with a progress indicator? What are the accuracy numbers per class?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is an optimization. I would first get per-class accuracy from the eval.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Most of the 13-point gap comes from the 25% hard class, so routing captures most of it. (b) A router misclassifies some hard queries. (c) Hard queries with a mid-size model plus a better prompt may reach acceptable accuracy.
  4. How I'd verify each: Evaluate both models per class; build a router and measure its confusion matrix; run end-to-end.
  5. Root cause: Averaging hides that the difficulty is concentrated.
  6. Fix (math): All-reasoning: 200k x $0.14 = $28,000. All-mid: 200k x $0.012 = $2,400. Routed (25% hard): 50k x $0.14 = $7,000 plus 150k x $0.012 = $1,800 = $8,800, plus the router (a small model, about $0.001 per query = $200) = about $9,000. That is slightly over $8k, so tighten: raise the cached-prefix savings, route only the hardest 20% (40k x 0.14 = $5,600 + 160k x 0.012 = $1,920 + $200 = $7,720). Accuracy: if hard queries are 60% on the mid-size model and 90% on the reasoning model, a 25% hard share contributes about 7.5 points of lift, so routed accuracy approaches about 88% on this assumption, which should be validated on the eval.
  7. Prevention: Monitor the hard-class share, router error, cost per query and accuracy per class weekly.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not use self-reported model confidence alone as the router; I would not route everything to reasoning for marginal gain; the 8 s latency needs a progress UI or async delivery.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Router sends 10% of hard queries to the cheap model. → Escalate on a verifier check or user retry, and tune toward recall on hard.
  • Reasoning price drops 50%. → Re-run the routing cutoff; maybe route more traffic.
  • Latency complaints. → Stream a status, offer async email for long jobs.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team moved everything to a reasoning model after a demo and watched the bill triple; routing recovered 85% of the gain at a third of the cost.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: single model, no numbers.
  • Hire: routes by difficulty with correct math.
  • Strong hire: validates the router, includes router cost, per-class eval, latency UX and monitoring.

questions.contextHtml: A travel-booking agent takes a median 38 s per request (users abandon after 15 s). Traces show 14 sequential steps per request: each step is a model call of about 1.8 s followed by a tool call of about 0.9 s (search flights, search hotels, get weather, get visa rules, price check...). Several tool calls are independent. The prompt grows each step because the full tool output is appended (context rises from 3k to 22k tokens). Total input tokens per request exceeds 150k.
questions.promptHtml: Cut the median to under 12 s without breaking quality.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a faster model." That gives maybe 20% and ignores the structure: 14 x (1.8 + 0.9) = 37.8 s.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which tool calls are independent? Is the plan mostly predictable (search, then price, then book)? Is booking part of this flow (side effects)? What does the eval say about quality per step?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stream progress ("searching flights...") and cap steps at 10.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) Too many sequential steps; (b) independent calls serialized; (c) growing context slows each model call and raises cost; (d) a big model used for trivial steps.
  4. How I'd verify each: Trace the dependency graph per request; measure model latency against context size; run the eval after each change.
  5. Root cause: Latency = steps x (model + tool). The design lets the model decide every trivial step one at a time and keeps all raw tool output in context.
  6. Fix: (a) Parallel tool calls: flights, hotels, weather, visa in one step (the model emits several calls at once) saves about 3 steps x 2.7 s per group. (b) Plan-and-execute: one planning call produces the plan; code executes deterministic steps without a model call. (c) Summarize or truncate tool outputs to the needed fields before appending (3k to 22k down to about 6k). (d) Use a small model for formatting or extraction steps. Estimate: 4 model turns (about 2 s) plus 4 tool phases (about 1 s) = about 12 s, then streaming progress hides the rest.
  7. Prevention: Per-step latency budget, an alert on steps per request, a regression eval for plan quality.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not parallelize dependent calls; I would not auto-book in parallel with unvalidated results; do not drop the agent for a rigid script if the cases vary widely, use a workflow for the common path and an agent for exceptions.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Tool APIs are slow (3 s each). → Cache stable data, prefetch likely calls, use async completion with notification.
  • Quality drops after summarizing outputs. → Keep structured fields the model needs; test with the eval.
  • Some users need the full agent. → Workflow for 80%, agent fallback for the rest.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An agent that "thought" about the weather lookup on step 9 could have been called in step 1 in parallel; one dependency diagram cut 24 seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: faster model or "add caching".
  • Hire: parallel calls, fewer steps, trimmed context, with math.
  • Strong hire: plan-and-execute hybrid, per-step budgets, safety of side effects and eval gating.

questions.contextHtml: Leadership asks you to migrate the support assistant (50k conversations a day) from a large model to a model that is 60% cheaper and 30% faster. A quick demo of ten chats looked identical. Your eval has 500 cases; the old model scores 88% resolution-correct, the new one 85%, but on the 60 adversarial and unanswerable cases the new model drops from 92% to 78% (it answers when it should refuse). Savings would be about $9k a month.
questions.promptHtml: Do you ship the migration? How?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "3 points is within noise, ship it" or "the demo looked fine". Aggregates hide that the failure is concentrated in the risky slice.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does a wrong answer on unanswerable questions cost (refund promises, policy misstatements)? Are there confidence intervals on the eval? Can we mitigate with prompt changes or a validator? Which traffic slices are low-risk?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Do not cut over. Keep the old model as the default.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) The new model is weaker at refusing; (b) the prompt was tuned for the old model; (c) eval noise (60 cases gives a wide interval of roughly plus or minus 10 points at the 78% level).
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-run with more adversarial cases, multiple seeds, and a prompt tuned for the new model; compute confidence intervals; analyse the failures by type.
  5. Root cause: A capability difference in calibrated refusal, hidden by an average.
  6. Fix: Route low-risk intents (order status, store hours) to the cheaper model, keep the large model for policy and complaint intents, or add a groundedness verifier to catch unsupported answers. Re-evaluate; ship by canary: 5% of traffic for a day, 25%, 50%, 100%, with automatic rollback if groundedness or escalation rate moves beyond thresholds.
  7. Prevention: The rule "every optimization is gated by the eval" with per-slice thresholds, and pinned versions.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not accept a savings-only argument; $9k a month is small compared with one policy-misstatement incident. Do not ship on a ten-chat demo.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Leadership says ship by Friday. → Offer the partial rollout: the low-risk slice now (about 60% of the savings), the rest after the fix.
  • The new model passes after prompt tuning. → Re-run the full eval, check for overfitting to the eval set, keep a held-out set.
  • Online metrics differ from offline. → Trust a canary with real traffic; check the segments.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cheaper model passed the average eval but over-promised refunds on policy edge cases; a per-slice gate would have blocked it before launch.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: ships on the aggregate or the demo.
  • Hire: looks at slices, routes by risk and canaries.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the eval uncertainty, ties the decision to risk cost, and sets rollback triggers and per-slice gates.
